title: Growing up in San Juan Hill
summary: He describes the West 63rd Street neighborhood as a rough but not poverty-stricken ghetto where kids fought their way to school together.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: By the way, where in New York were you born and where did you spend your early years?

Well, I was born in what was at that time called Sloane's Hospital for Women at, I believe, it that was at 60th 66th Street and Amsterdam Avenue. I lived at 246 West 63rd Street, which was just east of West End Avenue -- between West End and Amsterdam. And that's where I spent my early years.
Yeah. Was that the area called San Juan Hill?
It was not Hell's Kitchen, was it?
No. Hell's Kitchen was down, I believe, in the 40's -- in the upper 40's, south of there.
What kind of a neighborhood would you say it was in whatever terms you remember?

Well, it was what we would call, even now -- and even then -- a ghetto, you know. Not the worst ghetto. We weren't in too bad a shape. We weren't poverty stricken. I can't remember ever having to miss a meal.

But it was kind of a rough neighborhood, and, really -- not too rough. It was mostly rough -- leaving the neighborhood, going to school and back, you know, because we had to literally fight our way to school and back. I mean, usually the youngsters -- my contemporaries -- we'd have to meet on the corner and go to school together, you know?
